Rationale: Paper, waste, reuse, energy and resource-saving neighborhoods support the stable conserve sense.
Lifeguard and endangered-animal contexts support rescuing or saving living things from danger; preserve the stable rescue sense.
Transport, cinema, queue and manners contexts support the ordinary seat noun. Location, office and transitive seating dictionary senses are not current learner evidence.
Ball, basket, match, shot and goal neighborhoods explicitly support the sports shooting sense.
The Cambridge ability-list occurrence does not reveal whether shoot means a ball action, projectile shooting, or another dictionary use. Hold it rather than widening or guessing the learner sense.
Bathroom/take-a-shower and household water-use contexts support the bathing/shower learner sense; rain-shower and figurative senses are not evidenced.
Story-character and descriptive-adjective contexts support silly=foolish; the noun dictionary sense does not require a separate learner identity.
Toy/object neighborhoods support the skateboard noun. The action 'skateboard' is not independently evidenced as a separate elementary learning unit.
Slide followed by swing and seesaw is explicit playground-equipment evidence for the noun sense.
The PE/action sequence around kick, score, fly, skate, hit, warm-up and exercise supports slide as a movement action rather than playground equipment.
Both sources place sore directly with throat and health-problem vocabulary, supporting the physical-pain adjective.
The two current neighborhoods do not reliably distinguish place, mark/spot, or noticing/spotting. No elementary learner sense is assigned until stronger textbook context appears.
Shape, circle, triangle, rectangle and round neighborhoods support the stable geometric square sense.
City, street, sports centre, hotel and place context supports the stable public-square/plaza sense.
The Beishida Grade-1 flat-list occurrence still cannot distinguish geometric square from public plaza. Preserve the existing unresolved partition until evidence changes.
Postcard/collectible and counted-object contexts support the ordinary sticker noun; unrelated dictionary senses are not learner evidence.
